Where it began

Donald George Bradman was born in Cootamundra, New South Wales, on 27 August 1908, and was not yet three when the family moved to Bowral. Cricket ran on his mother's side: Emily bowled left-arm spin and had played in the women's intercolonial competition in the 1890s, and his uncle, George Whatman, captained the Bowral town team.

At home the boy made up his own game. Behind the house stood a water tank on a curved brick stand; he would throw a golf ball at it and hit the rebound with a cricket stump, over and over. He made his first hundred at 12, for Bowral Public School. Later, allowed only one week off work for a country tournament, he had to pick cricket or tennis, and picked cricket.

The player

His first-class debut came at the Adelaide Oval at 19, and he made a hundred. A year later he was in the Test side, and in his second Test, at Melbourne, he made 112, at the time the youngest man to score a Test century. In 1930 he took England apart: 254 at Lord's, which he thought the best innings he ever played, then 334 at Headingley, with 309 of them in a single day, and 974 runs in the series.

The big scores kept coming. In 1934 he made 304 at Headingley and shared a stand of 451 with Bill Ponsford at The Oval. In 1937, coming in at number seven on a drying pitch in Melbourne, he made 270, and Australia became the first side to win a Test series after losing the first two matches. In all he played 52 Tests from 1928 to 1948, scoring 6,996 runs at 99.94 with 29 hundreds. As captain he won 15 of his 24 Tests and lost only three, and he later led the side known as the Invincibles through a whole tour of England unbeaten.

What made him special

Quick feet, calm confidence and fast scoring were there from his very first innings. He was also wonderfully practical, and kept the ball on the ground because a ball on the ground cannot be caught, which helps explain why sixes were so rare in his game.

His bowling was a more occasional pleasure. He took two Test wickets, which suggests the batsmen of his day were relieved to see him with a ball in hand rather than a bat.

Away from the middle

For three decades after he stopped playing he served the game as an administrator, a selector and a writer. He was knighted, made a Companion of the Order of Australia and named an Australian National Living Treasure. His face appeared on stamps and coins, a museum devoted to his life opened while he was alive, and in 2009 he was one of the first players named to the ICC Cricket Hall of Fame. He died in 2001.

And finally

In August 1939 he won the South Australian squash championship. In the final he faced Don Turnbull, a Davis Cup tennis player, who led by two games and then had five match points in the third. Bradman saved them all and won. Some habits were hard to break.
